title: Complete Full-Stack Web Development Program
description: A full 20-module program from beginner to job-ready full-stack developer: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, Git, UI/UX, React, Node/Express, databases, auth & security, APIs, deployment, testing, AI tools, SEO, freelancing, 10 real-world apps, an industry capstone and a Certificate of Completion.
outcomes: Build responsive websites with HTML5, CSS3 and modern JavaScript
Use Git/GitHub and apply UI/UX design principles
Build interactive frontends with React (components, hooks, routing)
Build backends and REST APIs with Node.js, Express and databases
Add authentication, security, testing, deployment and CI/CD
Use AI dev tools, apply SEO, and build a portfolio to get hired or freelance
about: This is the complete TIH Full-Stack Web Development Program, rebuilt into twenty modules that take you from your first line of HTML to deploying full-stack applications.

Every content lesson has a video and printable notes with code snippets; ten real-world applications and an industry-level capstone build your portfolio, and you learn Git, testing, deployment, security, AI tools and SEO along the way.
You finish with a portfolio of deployed projects and — after the graduation assessment — a Certificate of Completion.
requirements: No prior coding experience required — we start from the basics
Willingness to type out and run the code in every lesson

faqs.question: How hard is coding for a complete beginner?
faqs.answer: This course is specifically designed for people who have never coded. We start from zero and progress gradually. Most students are surprised by how quickly they pick it up with the right teaching approach.

faqs.question: What tools do I need?
faqs.answer: VS Code (free), Chrome browser, and a free GitHub account. All are free and we provide step-by-step setup instructions in the first lesson.

faqs.question: Can I get freelance clients after this course?
faqs.answer: Many graduates immediately start freelancing. We include a bonus lesson on how to find clients, price your services, and deliver professional websites to Liberian businesses.

faqs.question: What should I learn after this course?
faqs.answer: We recommend our React & Modern JavaScript course for frontend advancement, or our Full-Stack Development course if you want to build databases and server-side applications.

instructor.name: David Weah
instructor.title: Full-Stack Web Developer & Tech Lead
instructor.bio: David Weah is a full-stack developer with 9 years building web applications for businesses across Africa and Europe. He has taught web development to over 2,000 students and runs a thriving tech agency in Monrovia.

Full-Stack Web Development · Module 1Course Orientation

Key Words & Meanings

Welcome to the Course

Welcome to the Course is the focus of this Course Orientation lesson. It develops the learner’s ability to apply this idea correctly in a working full-stack project and verify the result.

frontend

The part of a website users see and interact with in the browser.

backend

The server-side code that handles rules, data, security, and responses.

full stack

The frontend, backend, database, and deployment parts of one web application.

🧭 Welcome to the Course
Learn the concept, examine a working pattern, build it yourself, and verify the result.

Welcome to the Course

Definition

Welcome to the Course is a practical part of Course Orientation: the roles, tools, and workflow used to create websites and web applications. The lesson focuses on using it correctly, understanding the result it produces, and recognising when it is the appropriate choice.

Detailed explanation

A correct mental model helps a beginner understand how every later technology fits into one complete system. In professional development, Welcome to the Course should never be treated as isolated syntax. It connects to the user’s need, the surrounding system, and the evidence that proves the implementation works.

Before writing code, state the required result in plain language. Build the smallest correct version, inspect what happens, and improve it only after the core behaviour is verified. This reduces confusion and creates a process you can repeat on larger applications.

How the process works

  1. Identify what the browser, server, database, and developer each do.
  2. Install and verify the required development tools.
  3. Create a small file, run it, inspect the result, and save the work with Git.

Worked code or implementation example

<!-- A browser renders this HTML document -->
<h1>My first web page</h1>
<p>I am learning full-stack development.</p>

How to read this example: The example shows the normal pattern used in Course Orientation. Read it from top to bottom, identify the input or starting structure, follow the operation, and then find the output or result. Type it yourself and change one value so you can see which part controls the behaviour.

Professional best practices

  • Keep one organised project folder for each build.
  • Type commands and code yourself so the workflow becomes familiar.
  • Read errors carefully before changing anything.

Common mistakes and corrections

Common mistakeProfessional correction
Installing tools without checking their versionsKeep one organised project folder for each build.
Mixing unrelated project files in one folderType commands and code yourself so the workflow becomes familiar.
Copying code without running or understanding itRead errors carefully before changing anything.
💻 Practical task: Create a small example of Welcome to the Course in your own project. Run it, capture the result, explain one decision you made, and record one improvement you would make before production.

Real-world application

Developers use Welcome to the Course while building, reviewing, or operating real websites and applications. Add the completed example to a larger project so you can explain not only what the code says, but also what user or business problem it solves.

Summary

Welcome to the Course belongs to Course Orientation. A competent developer can explain its purpose, implement the core pattern, identify common errors, test the result, and connect it to the rest of a full-stack application.

Study tip: Type the example instead of copying it blindly. Predict what one change will do, run the code, and compare the result with your prediction.

Introduction to HTML is a practical part of HTML5: using semantic elements and attributes to give web content clear structure and meaning. The lesson focuses on using it correctly, understanding the result it produces, and recognising when it is the appropriate choice.

Detailed explanation

Well-structured HTML improves accessibility, search visibility, maintainability, and the reliability of every style or script added later. Before writing code, state the required result in plain language. Build the smallest correct version, inspect what happens, and improve it only after the core behaviour is verified. This reduces confusion and creates a process you can repeat on larger applications.

How the process works

  1. Choose the semantic element that matches the meaning of the content.
  2. Add necessary attributes, accessible text, and properly nested child elements.
  3. Validate the document and inspect it in more than one browser.

Worked code or implementation example

<main>
  <article>
    <h1>Course title</h1>
    <p>Clear, meaningful content.</p>
  </article>
</main>

Professional best practices

  • Use one clear h1 and a logical heading order.
  • Give meaningful alternative text to informative images.
  • Associate every form label with its input.

Common mistakeProfessional correction

Leaving images without useful alt textGive meaningful alternative text to informative images.

🎨 Introduction to CSS

Introduction to CSS

Definition

Introduction to CSS is a practical part of CSS3: controlling visual presentation, spacing, layout, responsiveness, and motion with cascading style rules. The lesson focuses on using it correctly, understanding the result it produces, and recognising when it is the appropriate choice.

Detailed explanation

CSS turns correct HTML into a clear interface that works across small phones, tablets, and large screens. In professional development, Introduction to CSS should never be treated as isolated syntax. It connects to the user’s need, the surrounding system, and the evidence that proves the implementation works.

Before writing code, state the required result in plain language. Build the smallest correct version, inspect what happens, and improve it only after the core behaviour is verified. This reduces confusion and creates a process you can repeat on larger applications.

How the process works

  1. Select the intended element with a stable selector.
  2. Apply layout and visual properties while respecting the cascade.
  3. Test the result at different viewport sizes and interaction states.

Worked code or implementation example

.card {
  display: grid;
  gap: 1rem;
  padding: 1rem;
  border-radius: 1rem;
}
@media (min-width: 48rem) {
  .card { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; }
}

How to read this example: The example shows the normal pattern used in CSS3. Read it from top to bottom, identify the input or starting structure, follow the operation, and then find the output or result. Type it yourself and change one value so you can see which part controls the behaviour.

Professional best practices

  • Prefer flexible layouts over fixed pixel positioning.

Common mistakeProfessional correction
Using overly specific selectors that are hard to overrideUse a consistent spacing and colour system.

button.addEventListener('click', () => {
  button.textContent = 'Registered';
  button.disabled = true;

In professional development, UI Principles should never be treated as isolated syntax. It connects to the user’s need, the surrounding system, and the evidence that proves the implementation works.

Before writing code, state the required result in plain language. Build the smallest correct version, inspect what happens, and improve it only after the core behaviour is verified. This reduces confusion and creates a process you can repeat on larger applications.

component

A reusable function or class that describes part of a React interface.

props

Read-only values passed from a parent component to a child.

state

Data owned by a component whose changes cause React to render again.

⚛️ Introduction to React
Learn the concept, examine a working pattern, build it yourself, and verify the result.

Introduction to React

Definition

Introduction to React is a practical part of React.js: building interactive interfaces from reusable components whose output responds predictably to data and state. The lesson focuses on using it correctly, understanding the result it produces, and recognising when it is the appropriate choice.

Detailed explanation

React helps developers organise complex interfaces into manageable pieces and update only what changes. In professional development, Introduction to React should never be treated as isolated syntax. It connects to the user’s need, the surrounding system, and the evidence that proves the implementation works.

Before writing code, state the required result in plain language. Build the smallest correct version, inspect what happens, and improve it only after the core behaviour is verified. This reduces confusion and creates a process you can repeat on larger applications.

How the process works

  1. Divide the interface into components with one clear responsibility.
  2. Pass data through props and keep changing values in appropriate state.
  3. Render the interface, handle events, and verify each state and route.

Worked code or implementation example

function CourseCard({ title }) {
  const [saved, setSaved] = React.useState(false);
  return <button onClick={() => setSaved(true)}>
    {saved ? 'Saved' : `Save ${title}`}
  </button>;
}

How to read this example: The example shows the normal pattern used in React.js. Read it from top to bottom, identify the input or starting structure, follow the operation, and then find the output or result. Type it yourself and change one value so you can see which part controls the behaviour.

Professional best practices

  • Keep components focused and reusable.
  • Treat state as immutable and update it with the provided setter.
  • Use stable keys when rendering lists.

Common mistakes and corrections

Common mistakeProfessional correction
Changing state variables directlyKeep components focused and reusable.
Putting every value in global stateTreat state as immutable and update it with the provided setter.
Calling hooks conditionally or inside loopsUse stable keys when rendering lists.

Definition

Introduction to Node.js is a practical part of Backend Development (Node.js): running JavaScript on the server and using Express to receive requests, apply application rules, and return responses. The lesson focuses on using it correctly, understanding the result it produces, and recognising when it is the appropriate choice.

Detailed explanation

Backend code connects the user interface to secure business logic, files, services, and databases. In professional development, Introduction to Node.js should never be treated as isolated syntax.   2. Validate input, apply the business rule, and call required services or data stores.
  3. Return an appropriate status code and response body, including errors.

const express = require('express');
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
app.get('/api/health', (req, res) => {
  res.status(200).json({ ok: true });
});
app.listen(3000);

Common mistakeProfessional correction

🧪 Browser DevTools

Browser DevTools

Definition

Browser DevTools is a practical part of Testing & Debugging: finding, explaining, preventing, and correcting defects through inspection, repeatable tests, logs, and performance evidence. The lesson focuses on using it correctly, understanding the result it produces, and recognising when it is the appropriate choice.

Detailed explanation

Testing and debugging turn code that appears to work into software that behaves reliably under expected and unexpected conditions. In professional development, Browser DevTools should never be treated as isolated syntax. It connects to the user’s need, the surrounding system, and the evidence that proves the implementation works.

Before writing code, state the required result in plain language. Build the smallest correct version, inspect what happens, and improve it only after the core behaviour is verified. This reduces confusion and creates a process you can repeat on larger applications.

How the process works

  1. Reproduce the problem consistently and record the exact conditions.
  2. Reduce the problem, inspect values, and identify the root cause.
  3. Fix the cause and run tests that prove the defect is gone without breaking other behaviour.

Worked code or implementation example

function total(a, b) { return a + b; }
console.assert(total(2, 3) === 5, 'total should add numbers');
console.assert(total(-1, 1) === 0, 'total should handle negatives');

How to read this example: The example shows the normal pattern used in Testing & Debugging. Read it from top to bottom, identify the input or starting structure, follow the operation, and then find the output or result. Type it yourself and change one value so you can see which part controls the behaviour.

Professional best practices

  • Test behaviour and outcomes rather than internal details.
  • Keep a minimal reproduction for difficult bugs.
  • Add a regression test after fixing an important defect.

Common mistakeProfessional correction
Changing several things before checking the resultTest behaviour and outcomes rather than internal details.
Ignoring the first useful error in a stack traceKeep a minimal reproduction for difficult bugs.
Testing only the happy pathAdd a regression test after fixing an important defect.

<title>Full-Stack Web Development Course | TIH</title>
<meta name="description" content="Learn practical frontend, backend, database and deployment skills.">
<img src="course.webp" width="640" height="360" loading="lazy" alt="Student building a website">

Common mistakeProfessional correction

Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Lazy Loading

Lazy Loading is the focus of this SEO & Performance lesson. It develops the learner’s ability to apply this idea correctly in a working full-stack project and verify the result.

SEO

The practice of improving content and technical signals so relevant pages can be discovered through search.

Core Web Vitals

User-centred metrics covering loading performance, responsiveness, and visual stability.

lazy loading

Delaying non-critical resource loading until it is needed.

⚡ Lazy Loading
Learn the concept, examine a working pattern, build it yourself, and verify the result.

Lazy Loading

Definition

Lazy Loading is a practical part of SEO & Performance: making pages understandable, discoverable, fast, stable, accessible, and useful to people and search systems. The lesson focuses on using it correctly, understanding the result it produces, and recognising when it is the appropriate choice.

Detailed explanation

Strong performance and clear content improve user trust, search visibility, mobile access, and conversion—especially on limited connections. In professional development, Lazy Loading should never be treated as isolated syntax. It connects to the user’s need, the surrounding system, and the evidence that proves the implementation works.

Before writing code, state the required result in plain language. Build the smallest correct version, inspect what happens, and improve it only after the core behaviour is verified. This reduces confusion and creates a process you can repeat on larger applications.

How the process works

  1. Define the user’s search intent and make the page’s purpose clear.
  2. Measure indexing, semantics, loading, responsiveness, and visual stability.
  3. Fix the largest user-facing problem and measure again.

Worked code or implementation example

<title>Full-Stack Web Development Course | TIH</title>
<meta name="description" content="Learn practical frontend, backend, database and deployment skills.">
<img src="course.webp" width="640" height="360" loading="lazy" alt="Student building a website">

How to read this example: The example shows the normal pattern used in SEO & Performance. Read it from top to bottom, identify the input or starting structure, follow the operation, and then find the output or result. Type it yourself and change one value so you can see which part controls the behaviour.

Professional best practices

  • Write unique titles and meaningful headings.
  • Compress and correctly size images.
  • Prioritise visible content and avoid unnecessary JavaScript.

Common mistakes and corrections

Common mistakeProfessional correction
Repeating keywords unnaturallyWrite unique titles and meaningful headings.
Optimising only for a test score instead of usersCompress and correctly size images.
Loading oversized media on small mobile devicesPrioritise visible content and avoid unnecessary JavaScript.
💻 Practical task: Create a small example of Lazy Loading in your own project. Run it, capture the result, explain one decision you made, and record one improvement you would make before production.

Real-world application

Developers use Lazy Loading while building, reviewing, or operating real websites and applications. Add the completed example to a larger project so you can explain not only what the code says, but also what user or business problem it solves.

Summary

Lazy Loading belongs to SEO & Performance. A competent developer can explain its purpose, implement the core pattern, identify common errors, test the result, and connect it to the rest of a full-stack application.

Study tip: Type the example instead of copying it blindly. Predict what one change will do, run the code, and compare the result with your prediction.

How the process works

  1. Publish a focused portfolio with live projects, source code, and clear case studies.
  2. Target suitable roles or clients with a tailored message and evidence.
  3. Agree scope, price, timeline, communication, and acceptance before starting work.

Worked code or implementation example

Project case study
1. Problem and target user

How the process works

  1. Write the user problem, essential features, data, and acceptance criteria.
  2. Build a small vertical slice, then add features in tested increments.

Common mistakeProfessional correction

🏆 Certificate Requirements
Learn the concept, examine a working pattern, build it yourself, and verify the result.

Certificate Requirements

Definition

Certificate Requirements is a practical part of Assessments & Graduation: verifying course completion, demonstrated competence, and the evidence required for certification. The lesson focuses on using it correctly, understanding the result it produces, and recognising when it is the appropriate choice.

Detailed explanation

A certificate is meaningful when it represents completed learning, successful assessment, and a finished capstone that can be verified. In professional development, Certificate Requirements should never be treated as isolated syntax. It connects to the user’s need, the surrounding system, and the evidence that proves the implementation works.

Before writing code, state the required result in plain language. Build the smallest correct version, inspect what happens, and improve it only after the core behaviour is verified. This reduces confusion and creates a process you can repeat on larger applications.

How the process works

  1. Complete the required lessons, projects, and assessments.
  2. Submit or present the capstone evidence to the required standard.
  3. Confirm the learner name and completion record before issuing the certificate.

Worked code or implementation example

Completion evidence
- Required lessons: complete
- Module assessments: passed
- Projects: submitted and accessible
- Capstone: evaluated
- Learner identity: confirmed

Type it yourself and change one value so you can see which part controls the behaviour.

  • Keep links and evidence for every required project.
  • Use the official learner name on the final credential.

Common mistakeProfessional correction

questions.question: Which tag creates the largest heading?
questions.explanation: <h1> is the top-level, largest heading.

questions.question: Semantic HTML means using tags that:
questions.explanation: Semantic tags convey meaning for accessibility and SEO.

questions.question: Which attribute makes an image accessible?
questions.explanation: The alt attribute describes the image for screen readers.

questions.question: A form sends data using the:
options: <form> tag with an action and method
questions.explanation: Forms use action (where) and method (how) to submit.

questions.question: Which element makes a hyperlink?
questions.explanation: The <a> (anchor) tag with href creates a link.

questions.question: CSS is used to:
options: Style the appearance of a page
questions.explanation: CSS controls colours, layout and typography.

questions.question: The CSS box model consists of:
questions.explanation: Every element is content + padding + border + margin.

questions.question: Flexbox is best for:
questions.explanation: Flexbox lays items along a single axis.
